glance: Forest Department permit and fees; included in tour packages
katka-kochikhali.desc: Katka and Kochikhali lie in the Sundarbans East Wildlife Sanctuary, near where the forest meets the Bay of Bengal. Grassy meadows, a wooden watchtower and walking trails to a wild beach make them highlights of overnight cruises. Herds of spotted deer, wild boar and many birds are common, and tiger pugmarks are often found. Both are reached only by boat on organised multi-day trips.
blocks: How to get there
Join a 2–3 day licensed cruise from Khulna or Mongla.
Good to know

Entry requires a Forest Department permit and armed guard, arranged by licensed operators. Walk only with the guard, in groups, and never at dusk. Do not swim at the beach: currents are strong. Avoid travel when cyclone signals are up.

glance: 190 km to Bagerhat by road, 5–7 hours by bus or car
Forest Department entry fee, approx.; plus boat hire from Mongla
karamjal.desc: Karamjal is a Forest Department station on the Pasur river, a short boat ride from Mongla. A raised wooden trail leads into the mangroves, where you can see breathing roots, crabs and monkeys up close. The station runs a breeding centre for estuarine crocodiles and river terrapins, and keeps spotted deer. It suits day-trippers who cannot spend nights on the water.
blocks: How to get there
Go from Khulna or Bagerhat to Mongla by bus, then hire a trawler from Mongla ghat (about 1 hr each way).
Good to know
Day trips here are permitted through the Forest Department station. Stay on the boardwalk, keep food away from monkeys, and hire only registered boats with life jackets.

glance: Hotels near Mongla port and on Sundarbans tour boats
mongla-sundarbans-crab.desc: Mud crabs are caught in Sundarbans creeks and also fattened in ponds near the forest edge. In Mongla and on cruise boats they are often cooked as a dry, spicy bhuna. Cracking the shells by hand is part of the meal. Ask for them in season and confirm the price before cooking.

glance: 190 km to Bagerhat by road, 5–7 hours by bus or car
kodla-math.desc: In Kodla (also called Ajodhya) village, about 8 km north of Bagerhat town on the east bank of the Bhairab, rises a brick math roughly 18 metres high. Its square base tapers into a curved rekha-style tower, a form linked to Odisha temple building, with niches and fine brick ornament on every side. An old Bengali inscription runs over the southern doorway. Local history credits Raja Pratapaditya, who built it as a memorial to his court poet Abilamba Saraswati; it is thought to be a memorial tower rather than a shrine to a deity. It is protected by the Department of Archaeology but sees few visitors.
blocks: How to get there
From Bagerhat town take an easy bike or motorbike north towards Baruipara union and Kodla/Ajodhya village (about 8 km); from Jatrapur bazar it is about 6 km east.
Good to know
Ask locals for 'Ajodhyar Moth' — that name is better known than Kodla. Go in the afternoon for warm light on the brick.

khan-jahan-ali-tomb.desc: Khan Jahan Ali, the saint-administrator who founded the town in the 15th century, lies in a single-domed tomb beside Thakur Dighi. Pilgrims come throughout the year, and the shrine has a steady devotional atmosphere. The pond has long been home to mugger crocodiles treated as sacred by visitors. A large fair gathers here each year around the full moon of Chaitra.
blocks: How to get there
About 3 km east of the Sixty Dome Mosque; take an auto or rickshaw.
Good to know
Cover your head and shoulders, remove shoes inside, and be wary of persistent donation seekers.

chunakhola-mosque.desc: Chunakhola Mosque is one of the smaller monuments of Khan Jahan Ali's era, a square brick building under a single dome. It sits away from the main road across rice fields, so few visitors make the walk. The terracotta decoration on its walls survives in places. The setting, with farmers at work around it, gives a sense of how the mosque city once blended into the countryside.
blocks: How to get there
From the Sixty Dome Mosque, ask locals for the field path; it is a short rickshaw ride and walk.
Good to know
Paths turn muddy after rain; wear sandals you don't mind getting dirty.

glance: Forest Department permit and fees; usually included in Sundarbans tour packages
dublar-char.desc: Dublar Char is a 66 sq km island where the Sundarbans meets the Bay of Bengal. Each year from October to March, thousands of fishermen from Khulna, Satkhira, Chattogram and Cox's Bazar set up camp here at spots such as Alorkol, Majher Char and Narikelbari. They catch and sun-dry Bombay duck, ribbon fish, shrimp and pomfret on long bamboo racks, making it the biggest dried-fish centre in the Sundarbans. The island also hosts the Rash Mela each November, when pilgrims come to bathe in the sea. Seeing the camps at work, with the forest behind and the open sea in front, is unlike anywhere else in the country.
blocks: How to get there
Only by boat, on a licensed multi-day Sundarbans cruise from Khulna or Mongla that includes Dublar Char (often around the Rash Mela).
Good to know
The smell of drying fish is strong; that is part of the place. Ask before photographing people at work, and keep to the paths your guide shows you.

dublar-char-rash-mela.desc: Each year on the Rash Purnima full moon, usually in November, pilgrims sail to Dublar Char at the southern edge of the Sundarbans. They bathe in the sea at dawn and worship, while a fair grows up on the sand. Through the winter the same island hosts large camps of fishermen who dry fish on bamboo racks. The festival is one of the few times large crowds enter the forest.
blocks: Good to know
Visiting requires Forest Department permission during the festival; boats get crowded, so travel with an organised group.

glance: 190 km to Bagerhat by road, 5–7 hours by bus or car
nine-dome-mosque.desc: The Nine Dome Mosque stands on the west bank of Thakur Dighi, the same pond beside Khan Jahan Ali's tomb, and dates from his governorship in the 1400s. A larger central dome is ringed by eight smaller ones, with round towers at the four corners. Terracotta flower motifs and scrolls frame the mihrab inside. It is part of the UNESCO-listed Mosque City of Bagerhat and is easy to add to a visit to the tomb.
blocks: How to get there
Walk along the bank of Thakur Dighi from Khan Jahan Ali's tomb; from Bagerhat town take a rickshaw or easy bike.
Good to know
Walk the full loop around Thakur Dighi in the late afternoon. The ruined Zinda Pir mosque and tomb are close by too.

glance: Varies by size, approx. 700–1,200 BDT per kg
Local hotels in Bagerhat town and Mongla
bagerhat-bagda-chingri.desc: Brackish-water shrimp farming shapes the landscape of Bagerhat, with flooded ghers stretching to the horizon. Bagda, the tiger prawn, is the main crop, much of it exported. Locally it is cooked in simple bhuna or with coconut, and small prawns go into vegetable curries. Eating it here, close to the ponds, is the freshest way to try it.

bibi-begni-mosque.desc: About 800 metres west of the Sixty Dome Mosque, on the west side of the large Ghora Dighi pond, stands the Bibi Begni Mosque. Local tradition says it is named after Bibi Begni, believed to have been Khan Jahan Ali's wife. It is a big square room under one dome, with walls about three metres thick, three mihrabs in the west wall and round corner towers banded with brick mouldings. It sits in the Chunakhola area, so you can walk on through the fields to the Chunakhola Mosque.
blocks: How to get there
From the Sixty Dome Mosque walk or take a van about 800 m west to Ghora Dighi; the mosque is on its west bank.
Good to know
Combine it with the Chunakhola Mosque on the same field walk. Paths can be muddy after rain.

glance: 190 km to Bagerhat by road, 5–7 hours by bus or car
Ticketed; foreigners pay a higher rate
sixty-dome-mosque.desc: Built under Khan Jahan Ali in the mid-1400s, the Shat Gambuj Masjid is one of the largest historic mosques in Bangladesh. Despite the name it has 77 small domes over its prayer hall, plus four corner towers, carried on rows of slender stone pillars. The terracotta-decorated brick walls stay cool even in summer. A small site museum nearby explains the wider mosque city.
blocks: How to get there
Buses from Khulna reach Bagerhat in about an hour; the mosque is beside the Khulna–Bagerhat road west of town.
Good to know
It is an active mosque: dress modestly, remove shoes, and avoid prayer times. Combine with Khan Jahan Ali's tomb the same day.

singair-mosque.desc: Singair Mosque lies about 200 metres south-east of the Sixty Dome Mosque, on the other side of the Khulna–Bagerhat highway. It is a square brick building under one hemispherical dome, with three doorways on the east, round corner towers and terracotta decoration on the walls. It dates from the mid-1400s and was in ruins before the Department of Archaeology took it over in 1975 and restored it. Because it is so close, most visitors to the Sixty Dome Mosque can see it in a few minutes.
blocks: How to get there
Cross the highway from the Sixty Dome Mosque and walk about 200 m south-east.
Good to know
Take care crossing the busy highway. Morning light on the east front shows the brickwork best.
